title: Este ou aquele? — shopping, colors and demonstratives
goal: Point to things at three different distances, name colors and sizes, then complete a purchase in a shop from start to payment.
bekal: using *ficar* to say something fits or suits you
naming colors that change form and colors that don't

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Na loja de roupa
dialogs.intro: Early November, and Lisbon is getting cold. Budi walks into a clothes shop in Chiado.

lines.speaker: Empregada:
lines.id: Good afternoon. Can I help you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sim, procuro um casaco. Está frio lá fora.
lines.id: Yes, I'm looking for a jacket. It's cold out there.
lines.literal: yes, I-look-for a jacket. is cold there outside.

lines.speaker: Empregada:
lines.text: Temos estes aqui. Que tamanho veste?
lines.id: We have these here. What size do you wear?
lines.literal: we-have these here. what size wears?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Não sei bem os tamanhos daqui. Na Indonésia uso M.
lines.id: I don't really know the sizes here. In Indonesia I wear M.
lines.literal: not I-know well the sizes of-here. in-the Indonesia I-use M.

lines.speaker: Empregada:
lines.text: Então pode experimentar este. É o M.
lines.id: Then you can try this one. It's the M.
lines.literal: then can try this. is the M.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Obrigado. Onde é o gabinete de provas?
lines.literal: thanks. where is the cabinet of trials?

lines.text: Tenho esse castanho e aquele azul-escuro, ao fundo.
lines.id: I have that brown one and that dark blue one over there, at the back.

lines.text: Gosto mais daquele azul. Quanto custa?

notes: **Fica-me apertado** — the verb *ficar* takes on a new job here: "to fit" and "to suit". *Fica-te bem* = "it suits you", *fica-me grande* = "it's too big on me". Note that the object pronoun attaches, exactly as in unit 12.

**Este, esse, aquele — three distances, not two.** Portuguese distinguishes things near the speaker (*este*), near the listener (*esse*), and far from both (*aquele*). English has only "this" and "that", so the three need practice. Think of *aquele* as "that one over there".
**Castanho, not marrom.** Brown in Portugal is *castanho* — from *castanha*, chestnut. In Brazil people say *marrom*. Likewise *em saldo* (on sale) in Portugal versus *em promoção* in Brazil.
**O gabinete de provas** is the fitting room. A shorter word that's also used: *o provador*.
**Que tamanho veste?** — *vestir* means to wear clothes, and its *eu* form changes vowel: *visto*. For shoes, the verb is different: *calçar*. *Que número calça?* = "what's your shoe size?"
**Precisa de ajuda?** is the standard greeting from shop staff. Note the *de* that's required after *precisar*, as you learned in unit 4.

grammars.title: The three distances of demonstratives
body: They all agree in gender and number with the thing pointed at — except the last form, which never changes.
after: **The last column is used when the thing hasn't been named or isn't known.** *O que é isto?* ("what's this?") — you don't know what it is yet, so you can't choose a gender. Likewise *isso é caro* and *não gosto daquilo*. These three never change form.
The matching words for place: *aqui* (here, near me), *aí* (there, near you), *ali* / *lá* (over there). Pair them up: *este... aqui*, *esse... aí*, *aquele... ali*.
**In everyday speech, people in Portugal often use just *este* and *aquele***, keeping *esse* for something the other person has just mentioned. If in doubt, those two are enough.

grammars.title: Contracted demonstratives
body: Like articles, demonstratives contract with *de*, *em* and *a*.
after: *Gosto deste* = "I like this one". *Gosto daquele* = "I like that one over there". Since *gostar* requires *de*, these contractions come up constantly when shopping.
The preposition *a* only contracts with the *aquele* group, marked with ` as in *à*: *àquele*, *àquela*, *àquilo*.

grammars.title: Ficar — to fit, suit and look good
body: This verb has now appeared three times in the module: "to be located" (unit 7), "to take (buy)" (unit 6), and now "to fit".

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: It's too big / too small on me.

after: *Melhor* (better) and *pior* (worse) are irregular comparatives. For other adjectives, comparisons use *mais* and *menos*: *mais caro* (more expensive), *menos caro* (less expensive), and the superlative adds the article: *o mais caro* (the most expensive).

blocks.text: **Colors that are really names of things never change form:** *cor-de-rosa* (rose-colored), *cor-de-laranja* (orange-colored), *bege*, *creme*. So *duas camisolas cor-de-rosa* — no *-s*. To say dark or light, add *escuro* (dark) or *claro* (light) after it: *azul-escuro*, *verde-claro*.

blocks.title: Portuguese clothing words that traveled the world
items: Portuguese traders left these words in Indonesian and Malay: *a camisa* → **kemeja**, *o sapato* → **sepatu**, *a renda* → **renda** (lace), *o saco* → **saku** (pocket), *o botão* → **butang** (button) in old Malay.
Watch out for *camisola*: in Portugal it means a sweater or long-sleeved top, while in Brazil the same word means a nightgown. One of those differences that can make a conversation awkward.
*As calças* is always plural, just like English *trousers* or *pants*. The same goes for *as meias* and *os óculos* (like *glasses*).
